blocks.text: A {blue|linear equation in one variable} is an equation whose variable appears only to the **first power**—no exponents, no square roots, no variable in a denominator. Every one of them can be rearranged into the form $ax + b = c$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are numbers.

items.note: The variable is raised only to the first power — linear.
Dividing the variable by a number is still linear.
The variable is squared — that's a quadratic, not linear.
The variable sits in a denominator — not linear.

blocks.text: **Solving** an equation means finding the value of the variable that makes both sides equal. On the SAT you'll solve equations directly, build them from word problems, and reason about *how many* solutions an equation has—this lesson covers all three.
Strategies

items: **Keep the equation balanced.** Whatever you do to one side, do to the other—always.
**Undo operations with their inverses** to peel everything away from the variable.
**Variables on both sides?** Collect the $x$-terms on one side and the numbers on the other.
**Asked for an expression** (like $6x - 10$)? Look for a shortcut before solving for $x$.
**Check your answer** by plugging it back in—or, on multiple choice, plug in the choices.

blocks.text: Inverse Operations
Every solving move is an **undo**. An equation was built by doing operations to $x$; you solve it by undoing them with each operation's inverse, working in **reverse** order of operations.

blocks.alt: Addition and subtraction undo each other
Multiplication and division undo each other

blocks.text: Think of solving as unwrapping: the last operation done to $x$ is the first one you undo.
To solve for the variable, isolate it: move everything else to the other side, one inverse operation at a time. Undo addition and subtraction first, then multiplication and division.
What value of $x$ satisfies the equation below?
**Check:** $5(7) + 7 = 35 + 7 = 42$ {green|✓} — the solution works.
Variables on Both Sides
When the variable appears on both sides, **collect the $x$-terms on one side and the numbers on the other**—then finish as usual.
What value of $x$ satisfies $2x + 9 = 4x - 1$?
Collect the $x$-terms on the side with the **larger** coefficient—here, the right side—so the coefficient stays positive and sign errors stay away.
Distribute First
If the equation has parentheses, **distribute before anything else**—then it becomes a familiar two-side equation.
Clear Fractions
A fraction is just a division—undo it by **multiplying both sides** by the denominator, ideally as your first move.
On multiple-choice questions you can also work backward: plug each answer choice into the equation and keep the one that makes both sides equal.

Some questions never ask for $x$. They give you an equation and ask for the value of an **expression**—and the fastest route is usually *not* to solve for $x$. Compare the target expression with the given equation first: it's often a multiple of it.
If $4x + 3 = 19$, what is the value of $12x + 9$?
Both routes work—but the shortcut is fewer steps, and fewer steps means fewer chances for an arithmetic slip.

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Before solving for $x$, compare the target expression with the given equation. If the target is a multiple of it, transform the whole equation instead of solving.

blocks.stem: If $3x - 5 = 16$, what is the value of $6x - 10$?

items.text: $7$ is the value of $x$ itself—the classic trap. The question asks for $6x - 10$, not $x$.
$21$ is the value of $3x$—stopping one step short of anything the question asked.
$6x - 10 = 2(3x - 5)$, so its value is $2(16) = 32$. (Solving instead also works: $x = 7$, and $6(7) - 10 = 32$.)
$42$ is the value of $6x$ alone—the $- 10$ still has to be applied.

blocks.text: When a question asks for an expression, the value of $x$ is almost always sitting among the wrong choices. Answer the question that was actually asked.
A linear equation in one variable doesn't always have exactly one solution. To find out how many it has, **simplify both sides completely** and look at what's left:
How many solutions does the equation $4(2x + 3) = 8x + 12$ have?
The $x$-terms vanished and left a **true** statement—the equation holds no matter what $x$ is. It has **infinitely many solutions**.
A Picture of the Three Cases
Treat each side of the equation as its own line: $y = \text{left side}$ and $y = \text{right side}$. A solution is an $x$-value where the two lines meet.

blocks.caption: The sides cross at one $x$-value.
blocks.alt: Two lines crossing at a single point

blocks.caption: Parallel sides never meet.
blocks.alt: Two parallel lines that never intersect

blocks.caption: Both sides are the same line.
blocks.alt: Two coincident lines drawn on top of each other

blocks.stem: In the equation $6x + k = 3(2x + 5)$, $k$ is a constant. If the equation has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $k$?

items.note: Identical $x$-terms — the constants must match too

items.text: $3$ is just the multiplier outside the parentheses, not the matched constant.
$5$ is the constant *inside* the parentheses—before the $3$ has been distributed.
After distributing, the right side is $6x + 15$. The $x$-terms already agree, so the equation is true for every $x$ exactly when $k = 15$.
With $k = 30$, subtracting $6x$ leaves $30 = 15$—a false statement, which means **no** solution rather than infinitely many.

blocks.text: Many SAT linear equations arrive as word problems. Nearly all of them are built from the same skeleton:

blocks.alt: Total equals starting amount plus rate times quantity

blocks.text: A moving company charges a one-time fee of $\$55$, plus $\$65$ for each hour of work. If a move costs $\$380$ in total, how many hours did it take?
Map the words onto the skeleton: the {green|total} is $380$, the {blue|starting amount} is the $55$ fee, and the {teal|rate} of $65$ per hour multiplies the {purple|number of hours} $h$:
The move took **5 hours**. Check: $55 + 65(5) = 55 + 325 = 380$ {green|✓}

blocks.stem: Amara puts $\$220$ on a transit card and spends $\$14$ from it each week. If $\$52$ remains on the card after $w$ weeks, which equation represents this situation?

items.text: Spending *removes* money: start at $220$, subtract $14$ per week, land on $52$. (Solving it gives $w = 12$ weeks—a reasonable number.)
Adds the spending, so the balance would *grow* each week—the opposite of the story.
Reverses the roles: it subtracts the starting balance from the spending, which has no meaning here.
Treats the leftover $52$ as the starting amount and the $220$ as the result—the story run backward.

blocks.text: Before solving, sanity-check the equation's *story*: should the total grow or shrink? Should the answer be large or small? A ten-second reality check catches most setup mistakes.
Solve each one fully before opening the answer. If you get stuck, name the move you need: distribute, clear a fraction, collect the $x$-terms, or scale the whole equation.

blocks.stem: What value of $x$ satisfies the equation $4x - 7 = 2x + 9$?

answer.text: **The correct answer is C.** Collect the $x$-terms on the left and the numbers on the right:

items.text: $1$ comes from subtracting $7$ from $9$ and halving—skipping the collection of $x$-terms entirely.
$4$ treats the equation as $4x = 9 + 7$, ignoring the $2x$ on the right side.
$16$ stops at $2x = 16$—the final division by $2$ is still needed.

blocks.stem: If $\frac{x}{5} + 3 = 10$, what is the value of $\frac{x}{5} - 2$?

answer.text: **The correct answer is A.** No need to find $x$: the given equation already tells you that $\frac{x}{5} = 7$, so $\frac{x}{5} - 2 = 7 - 2 = 5$.

items.text: Subtract $3$ from both sides to get $\frac{x}{5} = 7$, then subtract $2$ more: $5$.
$7$ is the value of $\frac{x}{5}$—one step short of what was asked.
$33$ is $x - 2$: it subtracts the $2$ from $x = 35$ instead of from $\frac{x}{5}$.
$35$ is the value of $x$ itself—the question asks for $\frac{x}{5} - 2$.

blocks.stem: In the equation $3(2x - 4) = 6x + c$, $c$ is a constant. If the equation has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $c$?

answer.text: **The correct answer is A.** Distribute, then compare the two sides:

items.text: With $c = -12$, both sides are the exact same expression, so every value of $x$ works.
$-4$ is the constant inside the parentheses—before it has been multiplied by $3$.
$4$ flips the sign of that inner constant on top of skipping the distribution.
$12$ is a sign error: $3 \times (-4) = -12$, not $12$. With $c = 12$ the equation has no solution.

blocks.stem: A climbing gym charges a one-time enrollment fee of $\$40$ plus $\$20$ per month of membership. Malik has paid the gym $\$240$ in total. For how many months has he been a member?

answer.text: **The correct answer is B.** Total $=$ fee $+$ rate $\times$ months:

items.note: Build the equation from the story

items.text: $6$ divides by the $\$40$ fee instead of the $\$20$ monthly rate.
$240 - 40 = 200$ spent on monthly dues, and $200 \div 20 = 10$ months.
$12$ is $240 \div 20$—it forgets the one-time enrollment fee.
$14$ adds the fee instead of subtracting it: $(240 + 40) \div 20$.

blocks.title: Things to Remember
items: Linear means the variable appears only to the **first power**. Solve by undoing operations—inverse operations, reverse order, and always the **same move on both sides**.
**Distribute** and **clear fractions** first; then collect the $x$-terms on one side and the numbers on the other.
Asked for an **expression**? Check whether it's a multiple of the given equation before solving for $x$—and expect the value of $x$ among the trap choices.
After simplifying: $x =$ a number → **one** solution; a false statement → **none**; a true statement → **infinitely many**.
Word problems: {green|total} $=$ {blue|starting amount} $+$ {teal|rate} $\times$ {purple|quantity}. Sanity-check the story before you solve.
**Check your answer** by plugging it back in—or plug in the answer choices.
